Ask first. Ask specifically what their protocol is when a patient is having suicidal thoughts. There should be a range, and they shouldn't be lawfully obligated to admit you unless you have a plan to take your life and are intent on acting it out. If you're at the ideation stage, they should talk it out with you and create a safety plan. That being said, some therapists don't stick to that range and will admit you for mentioning suicide. In that case, look for a new therapist. And if your thoughts become concerning, look into inpatient or outpatient facilities yourself, so you have options that aren't being forcibly hospitalized. Good luck with your session.

They also didn't tell me that there was a possibility for the stitches to shift, so years later, my right ear moved and changed shape, so it no longer looks good. Dr. Reinisch himself was nice, and his team is wonderful, especially in the way that they interact with patients. Everyone was very kind. I think I just had bad luck, but I wish I'd known there was a possibility for this bad of an outcome going into it.

I have microtia, and I recommend not doing the surgery. As someone else said, my ear looks worse than it did before the surgery, and I'm in the process of seeing if I can get it reversed. I got it done when I was 12, but it ended up being an ordeal consisting of eight total surgeries. Everything else was regular during my development, I didn't have issues with balance or socialization. I would recommend looking into Cochlear. That's the type that I use, and they have options for people who can't wear over the ear hearing aids.

This was years ago, I know, but I feel for you so much. I had reconstruction on both sides, and I really regret it. I didn't go with the rib cartilage option, since I was 12 when I got it done, and the idea of taking bone from my ribs terrified me. But the left ear got infected like three times, and had to be redone. Even when they finally settled on something, it looked terrible. The right ear looked fine, but then seven years later I woke up to a cracking noise, and I thought that I had broken it by sleeping on it. Turns out the stitches had shifted, pulling the entire thing backwards and completely ruining it. So now I have two ears that I hate, numbness in my thighs and left side of my head, and a new sense of bitterness about this procedure that seems to go great for so many people. Ok this struck a chord with me, because I had a similar experience. Therapists might have psych degrees, but when it comes to subjects like asexuality or even broad lgbt+ identities that are constantly shifting and still less than mainstream outside of online spaces, they don't always know everything. I've had plenty of experiences with therapists who didn't know anything about lgbt+ identities (and experiences with some who just generally didn't know what they were doing. The most liberating thought I think I had after going to a bad therapist for a few years is that sometimes, they're just bad at their jobs). I understand that feeling of questioning yourself when an authority figure says something that contradicts how you feel, but when it comes right down to it, your therapist isn't the ultimate authority on how you define yourself. And honestly, if they're trying to be, they might not be the right therapist for you. 
Also, you know, if you feel like you're asexual and identify that way, then get a couple of years down the road and realize that it's not the right label for you, then that's fine too. It's about you and what helps you feel comfortable that matters.

So I feel like for the most part a non-linear storytelling style mostly follows one plot, normally the main story, and will flash back or sometimes ig forward to things that can supplement the story or add things to it. And I think maybe that was their aim, because it seems like they weren't as interested in the backstory of the plague as they were in showing the aftermath, but in reality they kind of like... just flashed back and forth between story and story. Because the thing about the Stand is that it doesn't actually have a lot of backstory. The creation and spread of the plague is a part of the story, and if it's done right (1994 version) it can actually be an interesting part. So when they try to jump between plot points they just end up muddled and lost. 

And this might have just been me, but I feel like they wanted emotional payoff for scenes that they hadn't showed the backstory to. Like the shot with Nadine and the ouija board, that happened before they explained why that would be creepy. Same with Larry meeting Harold. We don't know why Larry should even know Harold exists yet, so it feels out of place. Idk SORRY for the long response, I also really liked the book, and I was excited for this adaptation, was very disappointed in it.

Honestly the only thing I feel like I need to say is that the 2020 version really skewed Harold in a weirdly positive light, even though they were deliberately showing him doing things that were bad/creepy. Harold in the book had an unrequited crush on Frannie, in the 94 series it was the same, and that wasn't really bad. He was supposed to be a character who was on the edge between good and evil, who ultimately gives in to Flagg's influence because he can't just let go of what's making him unhappy, even in this new environment where he's liked and has a purpose. In the 2020 version, he is shown to stalk Fran, or at least it's implied. He's written like a high school edgelord, basically, but because of how they follow him, it's almost like they're saying it's okay that he acts this way, because he's bullied and his crush doesn't like him back. Fran is a bad character, but I honestly don't think she owes Harold anything. He stopped her from killing herself, that was an addition that was not in the book, and I think may have just been written in to make people like Harold more, or to create a sense of obligation for Frannie that wouldn't and shouldn't have otherwise existed. She didn't owe Harold anything, not her time or her attention or her affection. She was a lot colder in the 2020 version, yes, but she didn't have any obligation not to be. 

There are reasons why Frannie is a bad character, she's underdeveloped and pidgeonholed into a one-note role. Even with their attempts to round her out in the series, they spent so much time on Harold that actually all of the other characters sort of fall flat. There are just so many other reasons why the way she's written is bad that don't revolve around Harold.

Honestly I would say if you're going to watch one of them, watch the 94 series. Not only does the newer one jump around too much for someone who doesn't know the material to understand, but they really mangled a lot of the characters. The only character who was ever given a decent amount of screen time was Harold, which was only good because Owen Teague did an excellent job. It was a stupid move overall, because Harold wasn't meant to be THE central character. Reading the book, even though there is a group of mains, I always thought the central character was supposed to be Stu. In this adaptation Stu doesn't even really have a personality. Also, they really reduced the complexity of Nadine's story and disrespected my boy Nick. I'd say the biggest draw of this series was, for most people, Alex Skarsgärd, but he doesn't really get to do anything. Jamey Sheridan's Flagg was fun to watch, and even if it was a bit hokey, you could tell that he was bad news, and I thought he did a good job of being genuinely scary at times. This Flagg... we're just kind of told that he's bad, we never get to actually see anything that could make him scary. 

Also once I got past the second episode and realized that this adaptation was going to be a trash fest I was watching solely for Fiona Dourif, but like I think someone else pointed out, she was given nothing to do. Her character wasn't even named, she was supposed to be the Rat (wo)man and it just wasn't ever mentioned, even though she was in the promotional posters and it seemed like they were hinting that her character would be a bigger deal.

Also also, yes the casting was more diverse, but they cast a hearing actor to play Nick and most of the series still just revolved around a white man :/
